subject: phy
title: Particle Physics
subtitle: Atomic nucleus, radioactive decay, nuclear equations and the Standard Model.
concept: The nucleus contains protons and neutrons held together by the strong nuclear force, which overcomes electrostatic repulsion at short range.
Radioactive decay is a random, spontaneous process; alpha, beta and gamma radiation have different ionising power and penetration.
Matter and antimatter can be created and annihilated; the Standard Model classifies fundamental particles as quarks and leptons.

notes.heading: Nuclear Structure
items: Nucleus: protons + neutrons (nucleons), radius ~10⁻¹⁵ m (femtometre scale); held by strong nuclear force.
Strong nuclear force: attractive up to ~3 fm; repulsive below ~0.5 fm; acts equally on p and n; short range.
Nuclear density: very high (~10¹⁷ kg m⁻³); approximately constant (independent of A).
Isotopes: same Z, different A (different number of neutrons).

notes.heading: Radioactive Decay
items: Alpha (α): ₂⁴He nucleus; charge +2; highly ionising; stopped by few cm of air or paper; deflected in fields.
Beta-minus (β⁻): electron emitted; n → p + e⁻ + antineutrino; moderately ionising; stopped by few mm Al.
Beta-plus (β⁺): positron emitted; p → n + e⁺ + neutrino; antimatter counterpart of β⁻.
Gamma (γ): EM radiation (high frequency photon); no charge or mass change; weakly ionising; attenuated by thick Pb or concrete.
Half-life (t₁/₂): time for activity (or number of undecayed nuclei) to halve; random and spontaneous.

notes.heading: Nuclear Equations
items: Balancing: top number (mass number A, nucleon number) must balance; bottom number (Z, atomic number) must balance.
Alpha decay: A decreases by 4; Z decreases by 2.
Beta-minus: A unchanged; Z increases by 1 (n → p).
Gamma: A and Z both unchanged (nucleus loses energy only).
Positron emission (β⁺): Z decreases by 1; A unchanged.

notes.heading: Standard Model and Particle Classification
items: Hadrons: particles made of quarks (baryons: 3 quarks, e.g. proton, neutron; mesons: quark + antiquark).
Leptons: fundamental; not made of quarks; e.g. electron, muon, neutrino.
Quarks: up (u, charge +⅔e), down (d, charge −⅓e). Proton = uud; neutron = udd.
Antiparticles: same mass, opposite charge/quantum numbers (e.g. positron = antielectron).
Pair production: γ → particle + antiparticle (energy → mass, E = mc²).
Annihilation: particle + antiparticle → 2γ photons (mass → energy).
Conservation laws in particle interactions: charge, baryon number, lepton number (and energy-momentum).

definitions.body: The short-range force (attractive at ~1–3 fm, repulsive below ~0.5 fm) that holds nucleons together in the nucleus, overcoming electrostatic repulsion.
The time taken for the activity (or number of undecayed nuclei) of a radioactive sample to fall to half its initial value; constant for a given isotope.
A process where a high-energy photon converts into a particle–antiparticle pair (e.g. γ → e⁻ + e⁺); requires photon energy ≥ 2m_e c².
A conserved quantum number: baryons (proton, neutron) have B = +1; antibaryons B = −1; mesons and leptons B = 0.

workedExamples.q: Write the nuclear equation for beta-minus decay of carbon-14: ¹⁴₆C → ?
A radioactive sample has activity 800 Bq. After 6 hours its activity is 100 Bq. Find the half-life.

mistakes: Forgetting to include the antineutrino in β⁻ decay equations (exam boards often require it).
Confusing baryon number (quarks) with lepton number (leptons) — they are separately conserved.
Stating gamma decay changes the nucleus — gamma emission changes energy but not A or Z.
tips: Quark composition: proton = uud (2×+⅔ + 1×−⅓ = +1); neutron = udd (1×+⅔ + 2×−⅓ = 0).
In β⁻ decay: d → u (quark level); in β⁺: u → d.
Pair production minimum energy: E = 2m_e c² = 2 × (9.11×10⁻³¹)(3×10⁸)² = 1.64×10⁻¹³ J = 1.02 MeV.

flashcards.q: What are the quark compositions of a proton and a neutron?
What changes occur to A and Z in alpha decay?
flashcards.a: A decreases by 4; Z decreases by 2.
The time for the activity (or number of undecayed nuclei) to halve; it is constant for a given isotope.

flashcards.q: Which is the most penetrating type of radiation?
flashcards.a: Gamma radiation — requires centimetres of lead or metres of concrete to be significantly attenuated.

flashcards.q: State two conservation laws that apply in all particle interactions.
flashcards.a: Conservation of charge; conservation of baryon number; conservation of lepton number; conservation of energy-momentum (any 2).
A high-energy photon converts into a particle–antiparticle pair (e.g. electron + positron): γ → e⁻ + e⁺.

questions.q: What is the quark composition of a neutron?
questions.exp: Neutron: udd (u=+⅔e, d=−⅓e); total charge = +⅔ − ⅓ − ⅓ = 0.

questions.q: Which radiation is stopped by a thin sheet of paper?
questions.exp: Alpha particles are large and heavily charged; stopped by a few cm of air or a sheet of paper.

questions.q: In β⁻ decay, which quark change occurs?
questions.exp: In β⁻ decay (n→p), a down quark changes to an up quark: d → u + e⁻ + ν̄_e.

questions.q: A sample's activity halves every 5 years. What fraction remains after 15 years?
Which particles are classified as leptons?
questions.exp: Leptons are fundamental particles not made of quarks: electrons, muons, taus, and their associated neutrinos.

recall: Describe the properties of alpha, beta and gamma radiation.
Write and balance nuclear decay equations.
State the quark composition of proton and neutron.
Define half-life and use it to calculate remaining activity.
